question.text: Given that $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]=-3,$ $\textrm {SD}[X]=3,$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]=2$, find the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y.$
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-3}{3\cdot 2} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align*}

question.text: The variances of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ are $0.09$ and $0.16$, respectively. Given that $\textrm{Cov}(X,Y) =-0.03,$ find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

In our case, we have

\begin{align*} \textrm {SD}[X] &= \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[X]} = \sqrt{0.09} = 0.3, \\[3pt] \textrm {SD}[X] &= \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[Y]} = \sqrt{0.16} = 0.4. \end{align*}

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[X]} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-0.03}{0.3 \cdot 0.4} \\[5pt] &= -0.25. \end{align*}

$X=1$ $0.2$ $0.6$ $0.8$
$f_Y$ $0.3$ $0.7$ $1$

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]=0.8\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]=0.7, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X] = 0.4, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y] \approx 0.4583, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\begin{align} \textrm{E}[XY] &= \sum\limits_{x \in S_X} \sum\limits_{y \in S_Y} xy \, f(x,y) \\[5pt] &= 0\cdot 0\cdot 0.1 + 0\cdot 1\cdot 0.1 \\[5pt] &\phantom{=\,} + 1\cdot 0\cdot 0.2 + 1\cdot 1\cdot 0.6 \\[5pt] &= 0.6. \end{align}

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &= 0.6 - (0.8)(0.7) \\[3pt] &= 0.04. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{0.04}{0.4\cdot 0.4583} \\[5pt] &\approx 0.22, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Continuous Random Variables

question.text:
\[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{8(x^2+y^2)}{\pi}, & \quad {x\geq 0,\; y\geq0, \; x^2+y^2 \leq 1} \\[5pt] 0,& \quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{8}{5\pi},\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{8}{5\pi}, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.2719, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.2719, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_{0}^1 \left[ \int^{\sqrt{1-y^2}}_0 xy \cdot \dfrac{8(x^2+y^2)}{\pi}\: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8}{\pi}\ \int_{0}^1 \left[ \int^{\sqrt{1-y^2}}_0 \left(x^3y+xy^3\right)\: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{8}{\pi}\int_{0}^1 \left[\dfrac14x^4y+\dfrac12x^2y^3\right]^{x=\sqrt{1-y^2}}_{x=0} \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{8}{\pi}\int_{0}^1 \left[\dfrac14\left(1-y^2\right)^2y+\dfrac12(1-y^2)y^3\right] \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_{0}^1 \left[\left(1-2y^2+y^4\right)y+2\left(1-y^2\right)y^3\right] \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_{0}^1 \left(y-y^5\right) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\pi}\left[\dfrac12y^2-\dfrac16y^6\right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{3\pi} \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{3\pi}- \left(\dfrac{8}{5\pi}\right)\left(\dfrac{8}{5\pi}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{50\pi-192}{75\pi^2}. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{50\pi-192}{75\pi^2}\right)}{(0.2719) \cdot (0.2719)} \\[5pt] &\approx-0.64, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.text:
\[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{x+y}{3}, & \quad {0 \leq x \leq 2, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1} \\[5pt] 0,& \quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{11}{9},\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{5}{9}, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.5329, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.2833, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^2 \left[ \int_0^1 xy \cdot \dfrac{x+y}{3} \: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3} \int_0^2 \left[ \int_0^1 (x^2y + xy^2) \: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3} \int_0^2 \left[\dfrac{x^2y^2}{2}+\dfrac{xy^3}{3}\right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3} \int_0^2 \left(\dfrac{x^2}2+\dfrac x3\right) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{3} \left[ \dfrac{x^3}{6}+\dfrac{x^2}6 \right]_{0}^{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3}. \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3} - \left(\dfrac{11}{9}\right)\left(\dfrac{5}{9}\right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{81}. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(-\dfrac{1}{81}\right)}{(0.5329) \cdot (0.2833)} \\[5pt] &\approx -0.08, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

example.title: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Continuous Random Variables

question.text:
\[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{2y}{x^2}+\dfrac12, & \quad {1 \leq x \leq 2, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1} \\[5pt] 0,& \quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{3}{4}+\ln 2,\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{7}{12}, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.2898, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.2764, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_1^2 \left[ \int_0^1 xy \cdot \left(\dfrac{2y}{x^2}+\dfrac12\right) \: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_1^2 \left[ \int_0^1 \left(\dfrac{2y^2}{x}+\dfrac12xy\right)\: \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_1^2 \left[\dfrac{2}{3x}y^3+\dfrac14xy^2\right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_1^2 \left(\dfrac{2}{3x}+\dfrac14x\right) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\left[\dfrac{2}{3}\ln x+\dfrac18x^2\right]_{1}^{2} \\[5pt] &=\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\ln 2+\dfrac12-\dfrac18 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2\ln 2}{3}+\dfrac38. \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &=\left(\dfrac{2\ln 2}{3}+\dfrac38\right) - \left(\dfrac{3}{4}+\ln 2\right)\left(\dfrac{7}{12}\right) \\[5pt] &=\left(\dfrac{2\ln 2}{3}-\dfrac{7\ln 2}{12}\right)+\left(\dfrac38-\dfrac{7}{16}\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{\ln 2}{12}-\dfrac{1}{16}. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\ln 2}{12}-\dfrac{1}{16}\right)}{(0.2898) \cdot (0.2764)} \\[5pt] &\approx -0.06, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician and integration by parts, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{\pi/2} \left[ \int_0^{\pi/2} xy \cdot \dfrac{\cos(x-y)}{2}\: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12\int_0^{\pi/2} \left[ \int_0^{\pi/2} xy\cos(x-y) \: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12\int_0^{\pi/2} \Big[xy\sin(x-y)+y\cos(x-y)\Big]_{x=0}^{x=\pi/2} \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12\int_0^{\pi/2} \left[\dfrac{\pi}2y\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}2-y\right)+y\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}2-y\right)-y\cos(-y)\right] \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12\int_0^{\pi/2} \left(\dfrac{\pi}2 y\cos y+y\sin y-y\cos y\right) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac12\left[\left(\dfrac{\pi}2-1\right)(y\sin y+\cos y)+\sin y-y\cos y\right]_{0}^{\pi/2} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\left(\dfrac{\pi}2-1\right)\dfrac{\pi}2+1-\left(\dfrac{\pi}2-1\right)\right]\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi^2-4\pi+8}{8}. \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi^2-4\pi+8}{8} - \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi^2-8\pi+16}{16}\\[5pt] &=\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-1\right)^2. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-1\right)^2}{(0.4332) \cdot (0.4332)} \\[5pt] &\approx 0.25, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

example.title: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Continuous Random Variables

question.text:
\[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac9{12}(xy+1), & \quad {y^2 \leq x \leq 1}, \, -1 \leq y \leq 1 \\[5pt] 0,& \quad \textrm{otherwise} \end{cases} \]

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that \[ \textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{3}{5},\qquad \textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{1}{7}, \qquad \textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.2619, \qquad \textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.4238, \] find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

\[ \rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}, \]

where

  • $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

  • $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

\[\begin{align} \textrm E [XY] &=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^2} xy \, f(x,y) \, \textrm{d}x \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_{-1}^1 \left[ \int_{y^2}^1 xy \cdot \dfrac9{12}(xy+1)\: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac9{12} \int_{-1}^1 \left[ \int_{y^2}^1 \left(x^2y^2+xy\right)\: \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac9{12}\int_{-1}^1 \left[\dfrac13x^3y^2+\dfrac12x^2y\right]_{x=y^2}^{x=1} \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac9{12}\int_{-1}^1 \left(\dfrac13y^2+\dfrac12y-\dfrac13y^8-\dfrac12y^5\right) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac9{12}\left[\dfrac19y^3+\dfrac14y^2-\dfrac1{27}y^9-\dfrac1{12}y^6\right]_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac9{12}\left[\dfrac19+\dfrac14-\dfrac1{27}-\dfrac1{12}-\left(-\dfrac19+\dfrac14+\dfrac1{27}-\dfrac1{12}\right)\right]\\[5pt] &=\dfrac9{12}\left(\dfrac29-\dfrac2{27}\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac19. \end{align}\]

Then, we compute the covariance and get

\begin{align} \textrm{Cov}[X,Y] &= \textrm{E}[XY] - \textrm{E}[X]\cdot \textrm{E}[Y] \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{9}- \left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8}{315}. \end{align}

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

\begin{align*} \rho &= \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]} \\[5pt] &\approx \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{8}{315}\right)}{(0.2619) \cdot (0.4238)} \\[5pt] &\approx 0.23, \end{align*}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.
